title: Beyond the Buffet: Indian Food Finally Gets Its Fast-Casual Moment in America
excerpt: From Curry Up Now's tikka burritos to Tarka Indian Kitchen's Texas expansion, Indian cuisine is carving out a fast-casual niche that the industry has predicted for years — and this time, the numbers suggest it's real.
body:
For years, food-industry forecasters have predicted that Indian cuisine would be the next global flavour to break through in America's fast-casual segment — the tier between McDonald's and fine dining that turned burritos, poke bowls, and Mediterranean wraps into everyday meals. For years, it didn't quite happen. The complexity of Indian cooking, the lingering association with cheap lunch buffets, and the sheer diversity of the cuisine resisted the kind of streamlining that fast-casual demands.

Now, in 2026, the breakthrough appears to be genuinely underway.

## The Numbers

The data points are converging. According to Technomic, 52 per cent of American consumers have tried Indian food and liked it — a figure that would have been unthinkable a decade ago. Datassential found that 49 per cent of US consumers have visited a restaurant that primarily serves Indian cuisine, though they may only go three to four times a year. The gap between trial and frequency is exactly the space that fast-casual concepts are designed to fill.

Indian food is now the second-fastest-growing global cuisine in America, according to Datassential. The US ethnic food market is estimated at $24.5 billion, and Indian food accounts for more than $5 billion in at-home consumption across the US and UK combined.

## The Pioneers

The entrepreneurs building this category have had to solve a problem that their counterparts in Mexican or Mediterranean fast casual never faced: how to simplify one of the world's most complex culinary traditions without stripping out the soul.

Tinku Saini, who opened the first Tarka Indian Kitchen in Austin, Texas, in 2009, believed Indian food had enough mainstream acceptance to work in a fast-casual model even then. "But it's not like burgers, pizza, or burritos," he told *Restaurant Business*. "The complexity of the cuisine was a gatekeeper to fast growth." Tarka now operates five locations across Texas and continues to expand.

Akash Kapoor, who founded Curry Up Now in 2009 — initially as a food truck — calls it "the Trader Joe's effect." The grocery chain's Paneer Tikka Masala, Lamb Vindaloo, and Vegetable Biryani have made Indian flavours as accessible and familiar as Thai or Mexican to mainstream American shoppers. Curry Up Now has grown into a multi-unit operation serving tikka burritos and deconstructed samosas across several states.

In Denver, Biju's Little Curry Shop has built a loyal following with a streamlined counter-service model. In Arizona, INDIBAR drew national attention as a 2026 James Beard Award semifinalist for Best New Restaurant — a rare honour for a concept rooted in elevated street food.

## The Perception Shift

What has changed is not just the number of Indian restaurants in America, but their cultural positioning. "Many Americans got their first taste of Indian food at mom-and-pop restaurants, often with cheap lunch buffets that weren't well maintained," Kapoor told *Restaurant Business*. "That negative impression stayed with them until recently."

The shift has been driven from the top down. When restaurants like Semma in New York win James Beard Awards, when Chai Pani becomes a household name, when Dhamaka lands on every critics' list — it resets the baseline perception of what Indian food can be. The fast-casual tier benefits from that halo effect.

Datassential has identified Keralan cuisine as its "Cuisine to Know for 2026," noting that 39 per cent of US consumers are interested in trying it. Regional specificity — South Indian dosas, Goan seafood curries, Himalayan momos — is replacing the catch-all "Indian" label, giving fast-casual concepts sharper identities and more distinctive menus.

## The London Factor

Adding fuel to the fire is a wave of imports from the UK, where Indian food has been mainstream for decades. Dishoom, the LVMH-backed Bombay café chain valued at nearly $400 million, is opening in lower Manhattan. JKS Restaurants is launching Ambassadors Clubhouse, a Punjabi concept, in New York, while its Gymkhana brand opened in Las Vegas. Asma Khan's Darjeeling Express and Kricket are also eyeing Manhattan openings.

Food Network named "imported international restaurants" its restaurant trend of the year for 2026, with Indian concepts from London leading the charge. These are brands that have already proven the model at scale in a market where Indian food competes on equal terms with French, Italian, and Japanese.

## The Diaspora Opportunity

For the Indian diaspora in America, the fast-casual wave means something personal. It means that the food of home — the chaat, the kathi rolls, the dosas — is finally being presented to mainstream America the way it deserves: with respect, at scale, and without apology.

The economic opportunity is significant too. As more Indian-American entrepreneurs enter the fast-casual space, they are building businesses that can scale nationally — creating jobs, generating wealth, and embedding Indian flavours deeper into the American culinary vocabulary.

## What's Next

The question is no longer whether Indian food can work in fast casual. It is how quickly the category can grow, and whether it can produce a true national chain — an Indian equivalent of Chipotle or Sweetgreen — that makes the cuisine a daily option rather than an occasional indulgence.

The ingredients are in place: consumer awareness, entrepreneurial energy, cultural cachet from fine dining, and a diaspora community that is both the core customer and the creative engine. The buffet era is over. The fast-casual era has begun.
